utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-14/2-A, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Appearances, please, for the Prosecution. Mr. Yapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: May it please Your Honour. I'm Upawansa Yapa, appearing for the Prosecution, with Mr. Norman Farrell. Ms. Edel Guzman is the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: For Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my name is Mitko Naumovski, attorney from Zagreb, and Defence counsel for Mr. Dario Kordic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: For Mr. Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. For Mr. Cerkez, Bozidar Kovacic, attorney from Milica Rijeka, Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kordic, are you able to hear the proceedings in a language which you understand? THE APPELLANT KORDIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, I can understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down. Mr. Cerkez, are you able to hear the proceedings in a language which you understand? THE APPELLANT CERKEZ: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down. This is a Status Conference called in accordance with the provisions of Rule 65 bis. Before we get to the matters which have been filed, is there anything which the Prosecution wants to raise generally?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Anything that is to be raised of a general nature on behalf of Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of a general nature, I have nothing to state. All I would like to do is to inform the Trial Chamber, if I may, that we filed two submissions yesterday. In view of the shortness of time, I'm not sure whether you have had a chance to look at them yet. Just so much for me, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I have looked at them. I must say, they were certainly very late. If you do want to raise these matters, it would assist everybody if you gave us a bit more time to look at them. But we have them. I'll deal with them later. On behalf of Mr. Cerkez. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm awfully sorry. [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have nothing special to raise. We have seen the submissions of the Kordic Defence. I was away when they arrived. I was on a trip. And I think that I can say that I agree with those submissions and perhaps will myself present additional arguments that is linked to the Bosnian archives, the archives in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to which we did not have access. Now we have obtained a document of this kind for the first time from the Prosecution. I am not ready today to engage in a discussion on the issue, unless we are going to discuss it within the frameworks of what was stated generally in the submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Before we turn to that, Mr. Yapa, can you please tell me what is the Bosnia-Herzegovina archive to which you refer in your letter?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: If Your Honour will bear with me, I'll give it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Your Honour be pleased. On the information that I have at present, I can say that it is - the document that was disclosed is the document that had been obtained from the Bosnian archives. I am not in a position to say as to when the document was disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I think you misunderstood me.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Your letter, which we got on an ex parte basis, to which I will return in a moment --

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: -- is dated the 13th the June, and it says: "The enclosed material is the result of our searches through the documents obtained from the ABiH archive."

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now that has produced this great mountain of paper. What I want to know is what do you understand to be the Bosnia-Herzegovina archive? We've had a lot to do with the Zagreb archive. That's obviously a different one.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: If I may go to the history of it as to how the document came to be disclosed on the basis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no. Please, Mr. Yapa. It's a very simple question. What is the Bosnia-Herzegovina archive? Is it a collection of documents which the Prosecution has obtained, and if so, when did it obtain it?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: I thank Your Honour. It is a collection of documents referred to as the Sarajevo collection, a document obtained from the ABiH archive during operation -- an operation in October 2000 and located in a shelf referred to as 5E7 in the ABiH 3rd Corps archive room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I don't think we need that detail. Now, you say that it came into the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor in October 2000; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: That is the information, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And was it ever disclosed to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: It was not. It had not been disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Why is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Your Honour asked me the question as to why it was not disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: The only -- the answer that I can give is that it had not been disclosed, and it was disclosed for the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But why was it not disclosed? is the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You see, you have an obligation, a continuing obligation under Rule 68 so that all material in your possession must be searched for documents which may fall within Rule 68, and if this collection of documents came into your possession something like eight months ago, the question is: Why was this document, which you disclosed on the 13th of June, not disclosed earlier?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes. The short answer I can give to Your Honour at this moment is that it had not come to our attention as a disclosable document at that stage. And when we were making a search for the documents that should be disclosed, we came across it and immediately we disclosed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Does that mean between October 2000 and June of this year there was no search being made through those documents pursuant to your obligations under Rule 68?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Particularly -- particularly for the purpose of Rule 68?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's right. It's a continuing obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: It is. It is. With respect, it is. So with that in mind, when the search was made --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: When was the search made? is the question. When?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: For the purpose of the disclosure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, look, please. When was the search made through this collection which you received in October last year for the purposes of Rule 68?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: The search or the attention given to documents is a continuing one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: So it came to our attention --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, look, please. I don't want these evasive answers. They may not be deliberately evasive, but they're not answering my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: When did somebody say, "We must look through this Bosnia-Herzegovina archive to comply with our obligations under Rule 68"?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: This has been so, with great respect, from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: -- from the very beginning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So as at October.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So somebody has been looking through those documents since last October, have they?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: It has to be so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm not sure that's an answer, however. Has somebody been doing it?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Your Honour, to give a very specific answer to that, I'm not in a position to do it now, but the assurance that I can give is the search has been going on, and when we came across the document we disclosed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: How large is this collection, the Sarajevo collection?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: I'm not in a position to give that answer at the moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, these are all matters that are very relevant to this. In that last decision that I gave in this case, I drew attention to the fact that it is very important. It is as important as the obligation to prosecute.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And the Prosecution having raised the description that they are ministers of justice, that is quite right, and one of the obligations they have as a minister of justice is to disclose to the Defence, not only pursuant to Rule 68 but a general obligation to disclose to the Defence material which will assist them. Now, in October of last year, the case was going.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And this was discovered for the first time in June. It seems that some explanation may be available, but it nevertheless will have to be given.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. Well, now, the application by Mr. Kordic for an extension of time. What do you want to say about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise, but I cannot but say something with respect to what the Prosecution has just said from when the document dates or, rather, from what time the Prosecution has the document in their hands. The Trial Chamber, on the -- in our case, on the 18th of July, 2000, issued an order to Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to supply the documents asked for by the Defence. The Prosecution knows full well -- has known full well for many years that we are seeking those documents. We ended our case last year in mid-December, and these documents were shown to the Court sometime in mid-October. That is to say, had they been shown in mid-October, by mid-October, I think the Trial Chamber would have made a different decision. So these are crucial documents, and that is why I cannot accept what the Prosecutor has just told us, that they had it in their possession as of October last year and that they disclosed it to us only with the letter that I received on the 14th of this month. So that is unacceptable to us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, if I may say so, you brought some of this upon your own head, because your application for the documents, the order for the documents, was made ex parte. So the Prosecution would not have even known that you were after those documents. It's not clear to me why it was made ex parte, just as it's not clear to me that none of this material that is attached to the motion is filed ex parte.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted -- let me start from the end. When I filed my motion, I wanted to make all those documents public, but I didn't want to be in contravention to a Court decision with respect to the storing of documents, so I wanted to ask the Trial Chamber to make all the documents public, because I was afraid that I would be transgressing in some way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There is a very wide distinction between documents being made public and being disclosed to the other party. Ex parte means that you have moved without telling the Prosecution that you have sought that order or that the order has been made, and I don't understand why that was done. Protective measures are to prevent material becoming public. That's a very different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We simply followed what the Prosecution did. The Prosecution also sought certain documents ex parte from some countries, and we did that with respect to third countries, the United Nations, and so on and so forth, so that it seems to have become standard practice by the Prosecution. And with respect to Bosnia-Herzegovina, at least at first, we wanted to come into possession of the documents for us to be able to work with them before presenting our evidence and case, and we undertook an extensive correspondence with the officials of the Bosnia-Herzegovina federation and the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina which did not give off any results, was not fruitful. But the Prosecutor did know that we were seeking these documents from Bosnia-Herzegovina, because we brought this up at a public session. Confidential annexes were perhaps not known, the annex was confidential, but it was common knowledge that we were seeking documents both from the United Nations and from other countries as well, the European Union, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The fundamental principle in every case is that ex parte proceedings should be entertained only where it is thought to be necessary in the interests of justice to do so, that is, justice to everyone concerned; where the disclosure to the other party or parties in the proceeding or the information conveyed by the application or of the fact of the application itself would be likely to prejudice unfairly either the party making the application or some person or persons involved in or related to that application. And I'm reading from a statement which has been repeated in many, many, decisions of this Tribunal. And if it has been the general practice, it's about time it stopped. But anyway, we'll have to deal with that problem later. My concern with your application is that if you do not put on your brief and the Prosecution works its very slow way through these documents, you are never going to put it on because there will be a constant dribble of documents. Why can you not put on your brief now, as you should, and when these materials become available, you will get a very sympathetic hearing to add those matters to your brief. But we have to get this appeal underway. Your clients are in custody, they've been in custody for a very long time, and the Appeals Chamber has to get on with its appeals.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept that absolutely, Your Honour, and I am ready and willing that all the documents filed ex parte previously to be available to the public, but I don't know what the fate of the discovery material was that we're receiving from the Prosecution, whether I can publicise it or not. So it was along those lines that I asked for instructions from the Court. But let me go back to the principle again, if I may, Your Honour. The document that we received on the basis of which we make our motion is a crucial document, because throughout our entire proceedings which went on for a full eight months, we discussed intensively persecutions, who attacked whom in the Lasva Valley, whether both parties and sides were ready or not. And so I was flabbergasted to hear that the Prosecution had in his hands the document in October last year, that is to say, before we wound up our case in chief, and that is a key document, to my mind. And on the other hand, the Prosecution has been given access and insight to the archive in Zagreb, as are we, so it is a minimum of equality of arms if we have the same the Prosecution had and we're hearing for the first time that those archives, in fact, do exist because the response we got from Herzegovina attached to the motion filed shows that that archive does not exist. Now suddenly it has turned up. I know that we filed our motion late yesterday, but let me try to justify myself by saying on the 14th of this month I received a letter from the Prosecution containing a document. On the 18th of this month, Mr. Kordic, in the afternoon, received the judgement in Croatian and I filed the Prosecution and the Cerkez Defence of these two motions on Wednesday, the 20th. Unfortunately I handed it over to the Trial Chamber yesterday. Of course, I don't wish to justify myself, and I'm sorry that Your Honour received the document only yesterday, but that's how things went. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'd like an answer to my question. Perhaps I'll ask Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. it in a different way. Have you got any other grounds of appeal other than the one based on this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we will be objecting, and we have several grounds for that against the judgement made which do not refer to this document, the one that we're discussing now. I apologise to the interpreters for going so fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Why is it, then, that you cannot file your appellant brief in relation to those other grounds of appeal?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what you're asking me now is contained in I think paragraph 11 of our motion, where we request additional time to file an appeal and not linked to insight into these archives, for the reasons we stipulate, and one of the reasons is that when Mr. Kordic read the judgement on the 18th, in the afternoon, and the 19th and 20th, I talked to him yesterday, we read it together, he found certain nuances in the judgement that he was not aware of until a few days ago, and he was not aware of it because I was not able to translate the entire judgement for him, nor was I able to feel these and note these nuances. I'm not ashamed to say that. And that is why I think in the interests of justice and in order to protect the rights of the accused to a fair trial, that now Mr. Kordic has himself read the judgement, he should be given more time to go into a study of the judgement and take note of some of the things he wishes to take note of. So we don't want 90 more days. What we are requesting for is an additional 30 days in that alternative case. But if I may just remind Your Honour that we feel that it is of crucial importance to see the archive, because the archive might determine --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Please. Please. I don't want you to repeat yourself. I'm asking you why you can't put on your appellant's brief by the time specified and add the material relating to that document later. Now, you say, do you, that you do not speak either English or French?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't speak French at all, Your Honour. I do speak English and I know it well enough for general purposes of communication, but the Registry of the Tribunal has not officially approved my English, nor do I know English sufficiently to be able to translate the judgement. And throughout the trial I used the Croatian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Then you might like to explain to me how you are qualified to appear as counsel in this case, because the Rules provide that you must speak one or the other of the languages unless there are special circumstances shown to the Registrar who rules that you may proceed in the Croatian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, this was applied for attorneys designated by the Court to be ex officio Defence counsel. I was appointed counsel by Mr. Kordic himself. But let me note that during the trial I had co-counsel from the United States, and of course English was their mother tongue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The Rule is quite specific, and it is of general application. It's not just those counsel who are assigned by the Tribunal to appear for an accused. Counsel shall be considered qualified to represent a suspect or accused if counsel satisfies the Registrar that he speaks one of the two working languages of the Tribunal. Now, that is of general application. And there is a proviso in Rule 44(B) that the Registrar may permit somebody who does not speak either of the two working languages of the Tribunal to appear where the interests of justice so demand, but I do not understand how you can say that you are here as counsel if you are not qualified to be so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, Your Honour, I am not quite sure that the Rule was in force in October 1997, when Mr. Kordic appointed me as his Defence counsel. That condition was not laid down by the Registrar at that time for me. Now, whether I'm qualified for the job or not, I don't wish to go into that and judge, but with respect to my knowledge of English, because the case is so specific and everything else, I had my colleagues to help me with my English, so we find ourselves faced with a very specific situation now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, but, Mr. Naumovski, what I'm trying to point out to you is that it is the -- the Rule about time for filing briefs proceeds upon the basis that counsel is qualified to appear, which means that he speaks one of the working languages of the Tribunal. Where there is -- where he appears as co-counsel, then it is usually regarded as being in the interests of justice that he should be allowed to stay there because he does have somebody who can read the judgements and such things. And I just find it slightly curious that being unqualified to appear as counsel, you are using that fact in order to get an extension of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I didn't wish to make use of anything, but I think -- I considered it to be my duty to ask for extra time because of Mr. Kordic and his ability to read through the judgement, and as I say, our Defence case was composed of individuals who have spoken Croatian and English for many years, but unfortunately I am the only Defence counsel left for Mr. Kordic at this point in time. I didn't want to exploit this as a fact, but I think that Mr. Kordic does have the right to be accorded at least that extra month for the reasons I have set out. Of course, with the Court's indulgence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, it needs more than the Court's indulgence, as you've put it, because it has already been made clear that the fact that the accused is unable to read the original version of the judgement does not prevent the time from running, although it is a matter to be taken into account in extensions of time. And it has already been taken into account. And at the time that that decision was given, it was indicated that the decision would be available in the course of this month and it has in fact been made available in B/C/S/ in the course of this month. So that's a fact that has already been taken into account. So paragraph 11 of your motion, frankly, does not cut much ice, to use a colloquialism. Is there anything else you want to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In respect of the motion, if you think there's no need to go back to the archives of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there is nothing else I really have to add, but if you do allow me a word or two about the archives in addition to what I've already said, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Naumovski, that is a matter quite separate. So far as I'm concerned, that is matter that you can add to your brief once it's filed, but that brief is going to be filed either at the time already specified or you might get an extension. It's a matter that I'll have to consult on. But it is -- nevertheless, you are going to put that brief on, and you will be granted leave, I can assure you, to add to it once you have been able to investigate the archives. The failure of the Prosecution to tell you about it before hand is a matter that will have to be taken into account in relation to that particular matter, but I'm worried at this stage only about your application for an extension of time. Now, there's nothing more you want to say about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well then. Well, now, Mr. Yapa, do you want to say anything in relation to, first of all, the ex parte nature of his documents? Even your letter has been filed on an ex parte basis, which I regard as complete nonsense.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Mr. Norman Farrell will make reference to that because we have material to indicate that earlier a document -- some document was filed ex parte and it was under seal and it was not made available to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Farrell.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Just with respect to your issue about the ex parte, the Prosecution agrees with your comments. It doesn't see any particular reason in this case why they were filed ex parte. With respect -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I am prepared to leave them on a confidential basis because they may well be matters subject to protection orders, but I propose, therefore, to direct that they be made available to the Prosecution. Is there any reason for all of these orders to be sought ex parte?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: On the basis of the material before you, at least at this stage it doesn't appear -- there doesn't appear to be, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But the Prosecution has in the past sought them ex parte.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: It appears that's the case, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And I'm not sure why.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: To be frank, I'm not sure why unless there is -- particular in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You see, if a state -- they could be made ex parte so far as the state in concerned. If you want documents from a state, you can get an order without them being heard. The Rule specifically provides for that. And if the state comes back and says, "We have security concerns," that clearly must be heard ex parte. But it seems to me that this practice that's grown up with both parties rushing off to Judges and getting ex parte orders has just got to stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I think we would probably agree with you to the effect that it's unnecessary, certainly. Just one comment. If we are requested to respond to this motion for the reissuing of an order to Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Not at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: No, no, no. I have no submissions to make on it, Your Honour, and we are not in a position to respond to the motion because we've just received it. If you are issuing an order that the ex parte nature be lifted and the matter be confidential, we will be in a better position, obviously, because then we can see the documents that are referred to. I'm not in a position -- I'm sorry, I don't know at this stage whether the order of the Trial Chamber issuing the order to Bosnia-Herzegovina and the basis for that order which is now under -- which is now referred to, whether that was ex parte as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: If we're to respond to this motion in writing, which we will do within the required time set out by the practice direction, if all that material could be made available on a confidential basis so we're in a position it to least assess it, to respond. That was the only comment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well, then. I shall make an order that the material which accompanied the motion will be made available to the Prosecution on a confidential basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is there anything that the Prosecution wants to say about the extension of time sought? Bearing in mind that it has a very real interest in the matter, which is consistent with that of the two appellants.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: The Prosecution is in a position and will be in a position with respect to our brief on August the 9th. The Court's previous order, in paragraph 16, referred to the extension on the basis that the B/C/S version was not available. The Prosecution, though it doesn't oppose strenuously, obviously if it's necessary in the circumstances of this case doesn't see a reason for the extension per se.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right, then. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I may add also the position of the Cerkez Defence on the same issue which was just discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: If you seek to join the motion, you will obviously have to file a document, but I'm happy to hear what you have to say in support of it. But you should take into account what I've already said, that you can get on with -- you've got other grounds of appeal, and you can get those -- the brief filed in relation to those grounds by that date in August. But if you want to say something about it, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honour. I shall formally join in this motion in writing, but since we are discussing its very substance now, I would like to add something to that which is specific from the point of view of the Cerkez Defence. In your first decision allowing us extension of time - and I studied it with due care to see which direction the whole thing was moving in, and today this was repeated once again - one of the key issues that seems to appear now is to strike a balance, it would seem, between the right of the accused to speedy trial and, on the other hand, his right to resort to all available means, including the time that is needed for preparing proper and good defence. This trial has been on practically since 1977 [as interpreted]. We think that quite a bit of time was lost in the pre-trial stage, but that is not important any more. The trial stage was very speedy. I would even say that it was too speedy and to the detriment of our defence, but even that is of no consequence right now. The point now is that right now, we are concerned in view of the rights of the accused concerning the speed of the trial. On the other hand, there are new documents. That is a fact. And now yet again we are extending that particular right or, rather, time. Are we, on the other hand, infringing upon his other basic right to defend himself properly? Another question I would like to bring up in connection with extension of time is a very practical issue in terms of preparing the appeal. I, for one, am working on this appeal in accordance with your recent ruling, and that is that it should be completed by the 9th of August this year. I'm specifically referring to one legal issue and two issues of procedure, and I'm working on that. Another group of issues that we are dealing with in the appeal is mainly factual matters. It has to do with the value of some of the evidence that the Chamber ruled on as they did. And I must say that in one or two places in the draft, after I received some documents from the Prosecution on the basis of Rule 68, exculpatory material, that is, and this was a package of 262 documents - I haven't seen the actual documents yet, but I've seen the list - once we saw these documents, we had to go back to that which was already written, and actually, we had to look at the whole matter in another way and to change it from a substantial point of view at one particular point. So is it opportune or is it rational for us to write that part of the appeal the way things stand right now, and then later, when we get new documents and perhaps when we carry out some new investigations in relation to some of the new documents, for example, the documents from the Bosnian archives, are we going to add extra passages with respect to certain very specific issues or not? Now, that is one of the dilemmas that I see right now. My conclusion and my proposal, if I may say so, is that if we look at the balance of these documents, I think that the right of the accused to prepare himself actively in the -- for working on the defence overrides the right to a speedy trial. I'm saying that because of the juncture that we are at right now, because we have been at trial for about three and a half years, almost four. Not exactly four but almost. So the time required should be extended, because I'm convinced that the force of the arguments presented and the method of approach applied will be far more expedient from the point of view of the appellant and, of course, from the point of view of the other party as well, notably the Chamber that will be dealing with all of these matters. My final proposal in this respect is based on striking a balance between these two rights that I have referred to. So a moderate period of time could be looked at, a month or two, for extending the deadline for presenting the appellant's brief, because otherwise we will not be in a position to use some of these new documents already in the basic appellant's brief, or then perhaps we could add something later, as you had suggested. Your Honour, may I just go back to the initial debate that you had with my colleague, Mr. Naumovski, and in part with the Prosecution, only in a sentence or two. Perhaps the Defence is in a rather unfavourable position because it asked for the Bosnian archives to be disclosed ex parte. It is a fact that in October last year, during the trial itself, it had to be quite clear, patently clear to the Prosecutor - and it was clear to everyone in the courtroom, I assure you - that there are documents from the Bosnian archives that are missing in the case, and that was quite clear. We had an imbalance in discovery - I think that by looking at all the files, you could have seen that for yourself - not only in terms of numbers, but also in terms of substance. We got the brunt of the documents we needed towards the very end. As far as my own defence is concerned, we got the most important documents once I had completed my Defence case, and in those days it was quite obvious that these were documents that were coming from one side but not coming from the other side, although both sides from the preparatory stage and the pre-trial stage were trying, in all possible ways, to reach the Bosnian archives. It is a fact that during the actual proceedings we did not have any new documents coming in from the Bosnian government or from the government of the Bosnian Federation, any of the entities. It was necessary to have these documents, and on the other hand, they were not Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. there. All of us together - the Prosecution, the Prosecutors, and we, the Defence counsel, either we personally or our own people - had access to other documents and we all brought them to this courtroom, but nothing came from the archives of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And that is the problem, that those documents that originated from the Bosnian authorities - I'm talking about predate in Bosnia - the first materials came with the indictment. But as soon as these materials became disputed, challenged during the proceedings, then no other documents came from Bosnia, and that causes great concern, Your Honour. And now when we got this letter from the Prosecution on the 18th of June, it is the first time that we see directly in writing that there are archives in Bosnia-Herzegovina and that there are relevant documents there. The first documents that we got had to do with the 7th Muslim Brigade, and it was referred to at least 200 times or 1.000 times. We can do this -- we can find the actual number of references in the computers. And now we get the first documents related to the 7th Muslim Brigade only on the 18th of June, 2001. So I abide by my original proposals, and of course I shall join Mr. Naumovski's proposal in writing as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And what will happen when the Prosecution produces another document that they have found in the course of their search through this archive? You will then ask for another month so that you can rewrite the whole of your facts. You have got to face up to reality in this, that Appeals Chamber is not unfamiliar with this problem that counsel want to do their briefs in the most perfect possible way and put them on only after they've had every opportunity to search for every document. But the Tribunal is obliged to get on with these things. Now, I can ask you: You do, I assume, have other grounds of appeal. You referred to a ground of -- a legal issue and two procedural issues. Those two can be dealt with and put on, and we want you to feel quite assured that there will be the opportunity to add other material if you are allowed to put in other evidence, or generally about the fairness of the trial. But there is no reason why you can't get on with something now, and all of the other material that you've put forward, so far as I can see, was implicit in your previous application. But anyway, it's a matter that, as I say, I will have to consult about. Is there anything more you want to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, nothing. But may I just add one more sentence? I absolutely concur with what you have just said. There would be no end to the proceedings involved if we were to reason this way. That is why I said that we have to find a realistic balance. In other words, to put it quite simply, when we see now that there are documents that I had already given up on personally - I thought we would never be getting them - let's see whether there is anything else left that is of crucial importance. And as you said in one of your rulings, it is in the cards. This dilemma will always exist. But do give us some time so that we can at least from the outset agree on the documents that exist. If other documents appear later, and I know that there will be other documents appearing later, let us not go back to Court every time and ask for further extensions. Of course, we can't do that, because then we would disrupt the balance I was referring to and then there would be no end to that. I am actually calling for a reasonable approach, because right now we have a situation whereby the documents have appeared. I don't want to go into all the details, but I also have four or five documents that are exculpatory, as the Prosecution had put it, for my Defence. But at any rate, we are talking about 262 new documents. Your Honour, right now I have no idea whatsoever whether I'm just going to file these documents in the farthest shelf in my office or whether among them there are 20, 30, or 50 really useful documents. I don't know. I am not asking for too much time, but I am asking for extra time so that we can see what we have actually got now, and then we can see what we can do with that. Then we file our appeal and then we see whether something else appears, and then perhaps we shall come up with additions. But as for the part that does not have to deal with facts, we are working on that, as expected, and we have nothing further to add in that respect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Can you tell me about these 262 new documents? You say you haven't yet received them or you haven't had the chance to deal with them?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have physically not received them yet. The OTP is very cooperative. They phoned me, I think it was this Tuesday. They phoned me to inform me that they have mailed a compact disk with these documents to me. We tried to stop this from both sides, because when you rely on DHL and other special postal services, it takes at least a week for me to receive these documents. My office is at the end of the world, so to speak. So I try to stop this, but to no avail. It's on its way. Yesterday the Prosecutors were kind enough to give me another copy, and I just looked at the headings. I looked at the documents. They are from the Zagreb archives, but it also has reference to exactly which file, which box it refers to. And there are titles of the documents involved, for the most part. So it's 262 documents. I looked at the list last night at the hotel and I see some very interesting documents there. I have to say that there are some specific subjects, for example, the detention of detainees. We have hundreds of documents in relation to that. But I see a few new documents in that respect. Perhaps they are of interest. I don't know, but I have to look at them. So I have certain reservations, but I see that there are some documents that could be very interesting from the point of view of their date as well. Because, Your Honour, we are dealing with a very long period of time in this case, but the bad things that happened in the Lasva Valley happened in April 1993 only, and that is why I focused on that month of April when I looked at this list, and I see that a lot of the documents refer to the month of April 1993. So I don't know. I expect there to be quite a few interesting documents here, and also I have high regard for what the Prosecution thinks in this respect. I'm pretty sure they didn't send me something that was pointless. I don't know whether you are familiar with the details, but before that, on the 24th and 25th, we got 8 documents; on the 31st of May, 18 documents; and on the 18th of June, the documents from Bosnia that we have been discussing today. I'm talking about the dates when I received these documents in my office, and all of them were sent a few days before that, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, at least we now have it on the record so that when you come back to us, if you do, again, we'll know something more about it. Thank you very much. Was there anything more that has to be raised? Mr. Yapa, do you want to raise anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: For Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Then a decision will be given on the motion. But so far as Mr. Cerkez is involved, you had better get that motion on as soon as possible joining in the application. We'll now adjourn.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Status Conference at 10.56 a.m.
